claim: Each k-fiber in HeLa cells in metaphase is composed of approximately nine KMTs.
source: Here, we show by large-scale electron tomography that each k-fiber in HeLa cells in metaphase is composed of approximately nine KMTs, only half of which reach the spindle pole.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and is supported by quantitative data from electron tomography reconstructions presented in the results section (Figure 3B shows 8.5 ± 2.2 KMTs per kinetochore, mean ±STD, n=292).

claim: Only half of the KMTs in HeLa metaphase spindles reach the spindle pole.
source: Here, we show by large-scale electron tomography that each k-fiber in HeLa cells in metaphase is composed of approximately nine KMTs, only half of which reach the spindle pole.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing that 49% (±15.5%, ±STD, n=3) of KMT minus ends were positioned within the MT-centrosome interaction area (Figure 5C).

claim: K-fibers exhibit remarkable variation in circumference and KMT density along their length.
source: We found that k-fibers exhibit remarkable variation in circumference and KMT density along their length, with the pole-proximal side showing a broadening.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative analysis of k-fiber cross-sections showing variation in polygonal area along the pole-to-kinetochore axis (Figure 7B).

claim: The pole-proximal side of k-fibers shows a broadening.
source: We found that k-fibers exhibit remarkable variation in circumference and KMT density along their length, with the pole-proximal side showing a broadening.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by measurements showing the average polygonal area of k-fibers was about threefold higher at the spindle poles compared to the kinetochores (Figure 7B).

claim: The association of KMTs with non-KMTs predominantly occurs in the spindle pole regions.
source: Extending our structural analysis then to other MTs in the spindle, we further observed that the association of KMTs with non-KMTs predominantly occurs in the spindle pole regions.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing that 60.7 ± 9.4% of KMT minus-end associations with MT lattices were observed at the spindle poles (Figure 8A).

claim: Mitotic spindles can contain thousands of MTs.
source: While mitotic spindles can contain thousands of MTs, only a fraction of those highly dynamic filaments is associated with the kinetochores (Redemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous work (Redemann et al., 2017).

claim: Only a fraction of MTs in mitotic spindles is associated with the kinetochores.
source: While mitotic spindles can contain thousands of MTs, only a fraction of those highly dynamic filaments is associated with the kinetochores (Redemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by both a citation (Redemann et al., 2017) and data from the current study showing only ~14% of all MTs were KMTs.

claim: KMTs function to establish a physical connection between the chromosomes and the rest of the spindle.
source: These MTs are called kinetochore microtubules (KMTs) and function to establish a physical connection between the chromosomes and the rest of the spindle (Flemming, 1879; Khodjakov et al., 1997; Maiato et al., 2004; Musacchio and Desai, 2017; Rieder, 1981; Rieder and Salmon, 1998).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: K-fibers in PtK1 cells are composed of about 20 KMTs.
source: Nevertheless, by applying serial thin-section TEM it was reported that k-fibers in PtK1 cells are composed of about 20 KMTs (McDonald et al., 1992; McEwen et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies (McDonald et al., 1992; McEwen et al., 1997).

claim: Tomographic analysis of RPE1 cells revealed 12.6 ± 1.7 KMTs per k-fiber.
source: In contrast, tomographic analysis of RPE1 cells revealed 12.6 ± 1.7 KMTs per k-fiber (O'Toole et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to a previous study (O'Toole et al., 2020).

claim: Different cell types can exhibit a wide range of chromosome sizes, which could be an important factor in modulating the number of attached KMTs.
source: Moreover, different cell types can exhibit a wide range of chromosome sizes, which could be an important factor in modulating the number of attached KMTs (Moens, 1979).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation (Moens, 1979) and inference from the observed variation in KMT numbers across different cell types.

claim: Single KMTs are connected to the kinetochores in budding yeast.
source: Single KMTs are connected to the kinetochores in budding yeast (Winey et al., 1995), while multiple KMTs are connected to dispersed kinetochores in nematodes (Oegema et al., 2001; O'Toole et al., 2003; Redemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous work (Winey et al., 1995).

claim: Multiple KMTs are connected to dispersed kinetochores in nematodes.
source: Single KMTs are connected to the kinetochores in budding yeast (Winey et al., 1995), while multiple KMTs are connected to dispersed kinetochores in nematodes (Oegema et al., 2001; O'Toole et al., 2003; Redemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies (Oegema et al., 2001; O'Toole et al., 2003; Redemann et al., 2017).

claim: KMTs in human cells are organized into bundles termed 'kinetochore-fibers' (k-fibers).
source: However, KMTs in these cells are organized into bundles, termed 'kinetochore-fibers' (k-fibers), which are attached to a single region on each chromosome (Begley et al., 2021; Godek et al., 2015; Inoue, 1953; Metzner, 1894; Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984; O'Toole et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Each metaphase spindle in HeLa cells was composed of approximately 6300 MTs.
source: Each of these metaphase spindles was composed of approximately 6300 MTs (6278 ± 1614 MTs, mean ±STD; Figure 2C–E; Table 1, Table 2) and had an average pole-to-pole distance of 9.0 ± 1.7 µm (mean ±STD; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-B; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by quantitative data from three full spindle reconstructions (Table 1).

claim: The average pole-to-pole distance in HeLa metaphase spindles is 9.0 ± 1.7 µm.
source: Each of these metaphase spindles was composed of approximately 6300 MTs (6278 ± 1614 MTs, mean ±STD; Figure 2C–E; Table 1, Table 2) and had an average pole-to-pole distance of 9.0 ± 1.7 µm (mean ±STD; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-B; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by measurements from three reconstructed spindles (Table 1).

claim: Between 90 and 110 k-fibers per cell were identified in the tomographic data sets.
source: In our tomographic data sets, we identified between 90 and 110 k-fibers per cell, which included on average 859 ± 218 KMTs (mean ±STD, n=3; Figure 2F–H; Figure 2—videos 4–6; Table 1) in each spindle.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by data from three spindle reconstructions (Table 1).

claim: Only ~14% of all MTs in the reconstructed spindles were KMTs.
source: Thus, only ~14% of all MTs in the reconstructed spindles were KMTs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and calculated from the data showing 859 ± 218 KMTs out of 6278 ± 1614 total MTs.

claim: The majority of annotated KMTs displayed open flared ends at the kinetochore.
source: The majority of annotated KMTs displayed open flared ends at the kinetochore (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), consistent with previous observations on the morphology of KMT plus ends in mammalian cells (McIntosh et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by visual inspection of tomographic data (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) and citation to previous work (McIntosh et al., 2013).

claim: The average distance between the sister k-fiber ends was 1.13 ± 0.24 µm.
source: The average distance between the sister k-fiber ends was 1.13 ± 0.24 µm (mean ±STD, n=292).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by measurements from all three data sets (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).

claim: K-fibers in HeLa cells are composed of around nine KMTs (8.5 ± 2.2, mean ±STD, n=292).
source: We further investigated the number of KMTs associated per kinetochore (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A; Table 3) and found that the k-fibers were composed of around nine KMTs (8.5 ± 2.2, mean ±STD, n=292).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by quantitative analysis of all kinetochores in the three reconstructed spindles (Figure 3B, Table 3).

claim: The number of KMT attachments to kinetochores in metaphase is not influenced by variation in the inter-kinetochore distance.
source: We did not observe a correlation between these parameters (Figure 3C–D; Pearson's correlation coefficients were 0.04 and 0.29) and concluded that the number of KMT attachments to kinetochores in metaphase is not influenced by a variation in the inter-kinetochore distance.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by correlation analysis showing no relationship between KMT number and inter-kinetochore distance (Figure 3C-D).

claim: The position of k-fibers within the spindle has no effect on the average number of KMTs per k-fiber.
source: However, we did not find a difference in the number of attached KMTs for these three different regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 3N; Table 5) and concluded that also the position of the k-fibers within the spindle has no effect on the average number of KMTs per k-fiber.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by analysis comparing central, intermediate, and peripheral k-fibers (Figure 3—figure supplement 3N, Table 5).

claim: The measured average kinetochore area was 0.10 ± 0.07 µm².
source: The measured average kinetochore area was 0.10 ± 0.07 µm2 (mean ±STD; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by indirect measurements of k-fiber cross-sectional area at the kinetochore (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-C).

claim: The density of KMTs at the outer kinetochores was 112 ± 60 KMTs/µm².
source: We then analyzed the density of KMTs at the outer kinetochores by counting the number of KMTs within the determined areas, which was 112 ± 60 KMTs/µm2 (mean ±STD, n=292; Figure 3—figure supplement 2D; Table 3).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by quantitative analysis of KMT density at kinetochores (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D, Table 3).

claim: The average center-to-center distance between neighboring KMTs is 74 ± 22 nm.
source: In addition, we observed an average center-to-center distance between neighboring KMTs of 74 ± 22 nm (mean ±STD, n=292; Figure 3—figure supplement 2E; Table 4).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by measurements of KMT spacing at kinetochores (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E, Table 4).

claim: The average wall-to-wall spacing between KMTs at the outer kinetochore is about 50 nm.
source: Considering an MT diameter of 25 nm, this corresponds to an average wall-to-wall spacing of about 50 nm between the KMTs at the outer kinetochore.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and calculated from the center-to-center distance measurement minus the MT diameter.

claim: The average length of KMTs is 3.87 ± 1.98 µm.
source: We also measured the length of the KMTs in our reconstructed k-fibers and observed a broad distribution of KMT lengths with an average value of 3.87 ± 1.98 µm (mean ±STD, n=2579; Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; Table 3).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by measurements of all KMTs in the three reconstructed spindles (Figure 4A, Table 3).

claim: About 20 ± 4% of the KMTs had lengths less than 2 µm.
source: Indeed, about 20 ± 4% of the KMTs had lengths less than 2 µm.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and calculated from the KMT length distribution data.

claim: About 39 ± 10% of KMTs were longer than the half spindle length.
source: Our analysis also showed relatively long KMTs (about 39 ± 10%) that were longer than the half spindle length.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and calculated from the KMT length distribution data.

claim: 49% (±15.5%, ±STD, n=3) of the KMT minus ends were positioned within the defined MT-centrosome interaction area.
source: Taking our determined cut-off value into account, we found that only 49% (±15.5%, ±STD, n=3) of the KMT minus ends were positioned within the defined MT-centrosome interaction area.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by analysis of KMT minus-end distances to the spindle poles (Figure 5C).

claim: The average number of KMTs per k-fiber at the spindle pole (4.1 ± 2.0, mean ±STD) was lower compared to the average number of KMTs per k-fiber at the kinetochore (8.5 ± 2.2, mean ±STD).
source: This is in accord with our observation that the average number of KMTs per k-fiber at the spindle pole (4.1 ± 2.0, mean ±STD; Figure 5—figure supplement 3; Table 3) was lower compared to the average number of KMTs per k-fiber at the kinetochore (8.5 ± 2.2, mean ±STD; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by quantitative comparison of KMT numbers at poles versus kinetochores (Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Table 3).

claim: Only half of the KMTs in HeLa cells are directly connected to the spindle pole, while the other half are indirectly connected.
source: All in all, this suggested to us that only half of the KMTs in HeLa cells are directly connected to the spindle pole, while the other half of the KMTs are indirectly connected.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and inferred from the data showing 49% of KMT minus ends within the MT-centrosome interaction area.

claim: Non-KMTs had an average length of 2.0 ± 1.7 µm.
source: Non-KMTs had an average length of 2.0 ± 1.7 µm (mean ±STD; n=14458; Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) showing a high number of very short (<2 µm) and a low number of long MTs (>half spindle length).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by measurements of all non-KMTs in the three reconstructed spindles (Figure 4B, Table 3).

claim: 38 ± 9% of the non-KMT minus ends were localized in the defined MT-centrosome interaction zone.
source: In addition, 38 ± 9% of the non-KMT minus ends were localized in the defined MT-centrosome interaction zone and the remaining ~60% were located in the bulk of the spindle (Figure 5E; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C; Table 3).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by analysis of non-KMT minus-end positioning (Figure 5E, Table 3).

claim: The average value of KMT tortuosity is 1.1 ± 0.1.
source: For all data sets, we observed an average value of KMT tortuosity of 1.1 ± 0.1 (mean ±STD, n=2579).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by measurements of global tortuosity for all KMTs (Figure 6E, Table 4).

claim: 62 ± 8% of the KMTs showed a tortuosity of lower than 1.1.
source: We found that 62 ± 8% of the KMTs showed a tortuosity of lower than 1.1 and 38 ± 10% of the KMTs displayed a tortuosity higher than 1.1 (Figure 6E; Table 4).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and calculated from the tortuosity distribution data (Figure 6E, Table 4).

claim: Straight KMTs (tortuosity <1.1) were predominantly located in the center of the spindle, while curved KMTs (tortuosity >1.1) were located more at peripheral spindle positions.
source: We also observed that straight KMTs (tortuosity <1.1) were predominantly located in the center of the spindle, while curved KMTs (tortuosity >1.1) were located more at peripheral spindle positions (Figure 6F; Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Table 5).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by analysis of KMT tortuosity by spindle position (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Table 5).

claim: The global tortuosity of KMTs was correlated with their length (R = 0.68; p = 2.2e-16).
source: Furthermore, the global tortuosity of KMTs was correlated with their length. As expected, short KMTs were straighter, while long KMTs were more curved (R = 0.68; p = 2.2e-16; Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by correlation analysis between KMT length and tortuosity (Figure 6G).

claim: 75 ± 6% of the KMTs with a tortuosity higher than 1.1 were longer than the half-spindle length.
source: In addition, 75 ± 6% of the KMTs with a tortuosity higher than 1.1 were longer than the half-spindle length.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and calculated from the combined analysis of KMT length and tortuosity data.

claim: The local tortuosity of KMTs was weakly correlated with the relative position of the KMT segments on the pole-to-kinetochore axis (R = –0.13; p = 2.2e-16).
source: Importantly, the local tortuosity of the KMTs was weakly correlated with the relative position of the KMT segments on the pole-to-kinetochore axis. The local tortuosity slowly and constantly increased from the kinetochores towards the spindle poles (R = –0.13; p = 2.2e-16; Figure 6I).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by correlation analysis of local tortuosity along the pole-to-kinetochore axis (Figure 6I).

claim: Cross-sections of k-fibers showed an average polygonal area of 0.097 ± 0.161 µm².
source: Cross-sections of k-fibers showed an average polygonal area of 0.097 ± 0.161 µm2 (mean ±STD, n=292).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by measurements of k-fiber cross-sectional areas (Table 4).

claim: The average polygonal area of k-fibers was about fourfold higher in the middle of the spindles compared to the position at the kinetochore.
source: Compared to the position at the kinetochore, the average polygonal area of the k-fibers was about fourfold higher in the middle of the spindles and roughly threefold higher at the spindle poles.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and calculated from measurements showing 0.034 ± 0.019 µm² at kinetochores versus 0.149 ± 0.210 µm² in the middle.

claim: At the spindle poles, roughly only 64% of the KMTs were enclosed in the defined k-fiber circle.
source: However, at the spindle poles, roughly only 64% of the KMTs were enclosed (Table 4).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by analysis of KMT density along k-fibers (Figure 7D, Table 4).

claim: K-fibers display a higher tortuosity and a lower KMT density close to the spindle poles compared to the kinetochore positions.
source: From all these analyses, we concluded that k-fibers display a higher tortuosity and a lower KMT density close to the spindle poles compared to the kinetochore positions, thus leading to a broadened appearance of their pole-proximal ends.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and inferred from the combined analysis of tortuosity and density measurements along k-fibers.

claim: Only 32.6 ± 5.5% of all KMT minus ends were associated with other MTs at an interaction distance of 35 nm.
source: Considering 35 nm as an example of a possible interaction distance between two MTs connected by a single dynein motor (Amos, 1989), we observed that only 32.6 ± 5.5% of all KMT minus ends were associated with other MTs (for a visualization of the pattern of association see Figure 8—figure supplements 1–2; Figure 8—video 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by analysis of KMT minus-end associations with MT lattices (Figure 8—figure supplement 1, Tables 6-7).

claim: 60.7 ± 9.4% of the total number of KMT minus-end associations with MT lattices were observed at the spindle poles (for 35 nm interaction distance).
source: As an example, for a given association distance of 35 nm, 60.7 ± 9.4% of the total number of associations were observed at the spindle poles.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by analysis of the spatial distribution of KMT minus-end associations (Figure 8A).

claim: 44.7 ± 5.2% of KMT minus-end associations with non-KMT lattices were observed at the spindle poles (for 35 nm interaction distance).
source: For the chosen distance of 35 nm, 44.7 ± 5.2% of these associations were observed at the spindle poles.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by analysis of KMT minus-end associations with non-KMT lattices (Figure 8B).

claim: On average 42 ± 8% of KMTs were associated with either KMT or non-KMT minus ends at 35 nm or closer to the KMT lattice.
source: At 35 nm or closer to the KMT lattice, we observed that on average 42 ± 8% of KMTs were associated with either KMT or non-KMT minus ends, with the majority of associations with non-KMT minus ends (Figure 8—figure supplement 3C-D; Table 8 and Table 9).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by analysis of MT minus-end associations with KMT lattices (Figure 8—figure supplement 3C-D, Tables 8-9).

claim: More than half of the KMT lattices (59.8 ± 6.7%) associated with other MT minus ends were preferentially found at spindle poles.
source: Again, more than half of the KMT lattices (59.8 ± 6.7%) associated with other MT minus ends were preferentially found at spindle poles (Figure 8C; Figure 8—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by analysis of the spatial distribution of KMT lattice associations (Figure 8C).

claim: Only 39.1 ± 4.6% of non-KMTs associated with other MT minus ends were found at the poles.
source: In contrast, only 39.1 ± 4.6% of non-KMTs associated with other MT minus ends were found at the poles (Figure 8D; Figure 8—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by analysis of non-KMT associations with MT minus ends (Figure 8D).

claim: Each KMT associates on average with 10.6 ± 3.2 other MTs in the spindle with an average association length of 145 ± 186 nm (for 35 nm MT-MT distance).
source: For a given MT-MT distance of 35 nm, each KMT associates on average with 10.6 ± 3.2 (mean ±STD, n=2579) other MTs in the spindle with an average association length of 145 ± 186 nm (±STD, n=2579).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by analysis of MT-MT associations (Tables 10-11).

claim: Each non-KMT associates on average with 7.4 ± 3.1 other MTs in the spindle with an average association length of 103±118 nm (for 35 nm MT-MT distance).
source: For 35 nm, each non-KMT associates on average with 7.4 ± 3.1 (mean ±STD, n=16256) other MTs in the spindle with an average association length of 103±118 nm (mean ±STD, n=16256).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by analysis of non-KMT associations (Tables 10-11).

claim: KMTs tend to show a higher number and a higher average length of associations compared to non-KMTs with increasing distance between MTs.
source: With an increase in the distance between MTs, we observed that KMTs tend to show a higher number and a higher average length of associations compared to non-KMTs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by comparative analysis of KMT and non-KMT associations at different distances (Tables 10-11).

claim: The number of KMTs per k-fiber in HeLa cells differs from previous observations in PtK1 cells.
source: Electron tomography revealed that on average nine KMTs are attached to each kinetochore in HeLa cells in metaphase. This result differs from previous observations in PtK1 cells (McEwen et al., 1997; O'Toole et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by comparison of current data with previous studies.

claim: About 20 KMTs were reported to connect to the kinetochores in PtK1 cells.
source: In this marsupial cell line, about 20 KMTs were reported to connect to the kinetochores.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous work on PtK1 cells.

claim: Kinetochores in HeLa cells are about half the size of kinetochores in PtK1 cells.
source: As previously observed by light microscopy, kinetochores in HeLa cells are about half the size of kinetochores in PtK1 cells (Cherry et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to previous work (Cherry et al., 1989).

claim: Kinetochore size in PtK1 cells was 0.157 ± 0.045 µm² as observed by electron tomography.
source: Similarly, kinetochore size in PtK1 cells was 0.157 ± 0.045 µm2 (mean ±STD) as observed by electron tomography (McEwen et al., 1998a), whereas kinetochores in HeLa cells, as determined indirectly in this study, have an estimated size of about 0.107 ± 0.075 µm2 (mean ±STD).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to previous work (McEwen et al., 1998a).

claim: Kinetochores in HeLa cells have an estimated size of about 0.107 ± 0.075 µm².
source: Similarly, kinetochore size in PtK1 cells was 0.157 ± 0.045 µm2 (mean ±STD) as observed by electron tomography (McEwen et al., 1998a), whereas kinetochores in HeLa cells, as determined indirectly in this study, have an estimated size of about 0.107 ± 0.075 µm2 (mean ±STD).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by indirect measurements from the current study.

claim: The area of the outer kinetochore might indirectly define the size and/or the number of available free binding sites for MTs.
source: Possibly, the area of the outer kinetochore might indirectly define the size and/or the number of available free binding sites for MTs (Drpic et al., 2018; Monda and Cheeseman, 2018).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion as speculation and supported by citations to previous work (Drpic et al., 2018; Monda and Cheeseman, 2018).

claim: KMTs in reconstructed k-fibers are of different lengths, confirming previous observations.
source: KMTs in our reconstructed k-fibers are of different lengths, confirming previous observations (McDonald et al., 1992; O'Toole et al., 2020; Sikirzhytski et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by current data and citations to previous studies.

claim: K-fibers in HeLa cells mediate a semi-direct connection with the spindle poles.
source: In agreement with previously published data (McDonald et al., 1992; O'Toole et al., 2020), our tomographic analysis of mammalian KMTs thus suggests that the k-fibers in HeLa cells mediate a semi-direct connection with the spindle poles, in which at least one KMT of the k-fibers is directly connected to the poles, while the other KMTs of the fiber are indirectly linked to non-KMTs (Figure 10).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by current data showing variable KMT lengths and minus-end positioning, as well as citations to previous work.

claim: Spindles in nematode embryos and in mammalian cells are similar in that anchoring of KMTs into the spindle network can be observed.
source: Thus, spindles in nematode embryos and in mammalian cells are similar in that anchoring of KMTs into the spindle network can be observed.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and inferred from comparison of current data with previous work on C. elegans.

claim: Centrally located KMTs were shorter, and their minus ends showed a shorter distance to the mother centriole compared to peripheral KMTs.
source: Interestingly, we observed a difference in KMT length and their minus-end distance to the pole in central versus peripheral KMTs. Centrally located KMTs were shorter, and their minus ends showed a shorter distance to the mother centriole compared to peripheral KMTs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by data from positional analysis of KMTs (Figure 5—figure supplement 4, Table 5).

claim: The difference in KMT length and minus-end distance between central and peripheral KMTs is most likely related to the roundedness of the mitotic spindles.
source: This difference is most likely related to the roundedness of the mitotic spindles (Taubenberger et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion as inference and supported by a citation (Taubenberger et al., 2020).

claim: KMTs in HeLa cells show a length distribution that is strikingly similar to the distribution obtained by biophysical modeling in combination with light microscopy.
source: Essentially, our 3D reconstructions show a distribution of KMT length in metaphase that is strikingly similar to the distribution plot of KMT length as obtained by biophysical modeling in combination with light microscopy (see Figure 8B-D in Conway et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by comparison with a parallel study (Conway et al., 2022).

claim: Only ~14% of all MTs in the reconstructed spindles were KMTs, but this corresponds to ~25% of the tubulin mass.
source: Counting the total number of KMTs and non-KMTs in our spindles, we show that only ~14% of all MTs in the reconstructed spindles were KMTs. However, this percentage in the total number of all MTs corresponds to ~25% of the tubulin mass as measured in parallel by light microscopy (Conway et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by current data and comparison with light microscopy measurements from a parallel study (Conway et al., 2022).

claim: KMTs are on average twice as long as non-KMTs.
source: Comparing the average length of KMTs and non-KMTs, we also find that KMTs are on average twice as long as non-KMT.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and calculated from the data showing KMT average length of 3.87 µm versus non-KMT average length of 2.0 µm.

claim: The length distribution of KMTs in HeLa cells shows striking similarities to the distribution of KMTs observed in the early C. elegans embryo.
source: The length distribution of KMTs in HeLa cells shows striking similarities to the distribution of KMTs observed in the early C. elegans embryo (Redemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by comparison with previous work (Redemann et al., 2017).

claim: About 57% of the non-KMTs and ~21% of KMTs in HeLa cells were less than 2 µm in length.
source: In contrast, non-KMTs in both systems show an exponential length distribution with a very high occurrence of very short MTs (around 57% of the non-KMTs and ~21% of KMT in HeLa cells were less than 2 µm in length).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and calculated from the length distribution data.

claim: Exponential length distributions as found for non-KMTs are typical of dynamic instability kinetics.
source: Exponential length distributions as found for non-KMTs are typical of dynamic instability kinetics (Burbank et al., 2007; Loiodice et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous work (Burbank et al., 2007; Loiodice et al., 2019).

claim: The observed length distribution of KMTs indicates a difference in dynamics and possibly higher stability of the plus-ends against MT depolymerization.
source: The observed length distribution of KMTs, however, indicates a difference in dynamics and possibly higher stability of the plus-ends against MT depolymerization.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and inferred from the comparison of KMT and non-KMT length distributions.

claim: KMTs in both HeLa and C. elegans spindles have distinct properties different from those of non-KMTs.
source: Taken together, all this argues that KMTs in both spindles have distinct properties different from those of non-KMTs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and inferred from the comparative analysis of KMT and non-KMT properties.

claim: Cold-treated cells show cold-stable k-fibers, while most of the non-KMTs undergo depolymerization upon exposure to cold.
source: Such treated cells show cold-stable k-fibers, while most of the non-KMTs undergo depolymerization upon exposure to cold (Maiato et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to previous work (Maiato et al., 2004).

claim: KMTs are likely stabilized by interaction with the kinetochores.
source: Likely, KMTs are stabilized by interaction with the kinetochores (Brinkley and Cartwright, 1975; DeLuca et al., 2006; Warren et al., 2020) and/or by KMT-KMT/KMT-non-KMT associations, possibly mediated by several MT-associated proteins (Agarwal, 2018).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion as speculation and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The difference in the number of attached KMTs between HeLa and PtK1 cells could be related to kinetochore size.
source: This difference in the number of attached KMTs could be related to kinetochore size.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and inferred from the comparison of kinetochore sizes and KMT numbers between cell types.

claim: The number of KMTs per k-fiber is not related to the position of these KMTs in the spindles.
source: Concerning the number of kinetochore-attached MTs, it is interesting to note here that the number of KMTs per k-fiber is not related to the position of these KMTs in the spindles.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by data showing similar KMT numbers for central, intermediate, and peripheral k-fibers.

claim: The peripheral position of k-fibers within the spindle accompanied by an increase in the global tortuosity has no effect on the number of KMTs in the k-fibers.
source: Thus, the peripheral position of k-fibers within the spindle accompanied by an increase in the global tortuosity has no effect on the number of KMTs in the k-fibers.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and inferred from the data showing no correlation between k-fiber position and KMT number.

claim: Many KMTs are relatively short with ~20% of KMTs shorter than 2 µm.
source: In fact, many KMTs are relatively short (~20% of KMTs were shorter than 2 µm; Figure 4A), and half of the KMT minus ends are not positioned in the defined MT-centrosome interaction area.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by data from the length distribution analysis (Figure 4A).

claim: Only 5% of the analyzed k-fibers show a length distribution in which none of the analyzed KMTs is positioned in the MT-centrosome interaction area.
source: Interestingly, only 5% of the analyzed k-fibers show a length distribution in which none of the analyzed KMTs is positioned in the MT-centrosome interaction area (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and calculated from the data on KMT minus-end positioning (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).

claim: In C. elegans, only about 20% of the KMT minus ends were located within 2 µm of their corresponding mother centriole.
source: When analyzing KMTs in the one-cell C. elegans embryo, we found that only about 20% of the KMT minus ends were located within 2 µm of their corresponding mother centriole.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by reference to previous work on C. elegans.

claim: The majority of KMTs in C. elegans do not contact the centrosomes.
source: This suggested that the majority of KMTs in C. elegans do not contact the centrosomes.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and inferred from the data on C. elegans KMT minus-end positioning.

claim: The position of the k-fibers within the spindle affects the ultrastructure of the individual KMTs.
source: This suggested to us that the position of the k-fibers within the spindle affects the ultrastructure of the individual KMTs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and inferred from the observed differences in KMT length and minus-end distance between central and peripheral k-fibers.

claim: An increase in the tortuosity of KMTs at spindle poles might promote the anchoring of the broadened k-fibers into the non-KMT network through MT-MT interactions.
source: An increase in the tortuosity of KMTs at spindle poles might promote the anchoring of the broadened k-fibers into the non-KMT network through MT-MT interactions (Figure 10C–D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion as speculation and supported by the observed correlation between tortuosity and MT-MT interactions at poles.

claim: The observed organization of KMTs in k-fibers is likely the result of KMTs interacting with other non-KMTs in the spindle.
source: Likely, the observed organization of KMTs in k-fibers is the result of KMTs interacting with other non-KMTs in the spindle, thus contributing to the maturing of k-fibers (Almeida et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion as inference and supported by a citation (Almeida et al., 2021).

claim: KMTs show a high tendency to associate with non-KMTs at the spindle poles.
source: In contrast to non-KMTs, KMTs show a high tendency to associate with non-KMTs at the spindle poles (Figure 8F–G; Figure 9C–D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by data showing preferential association of KMTs with other MTs at poles (Figures 8, 9).

claim: Non-KMTs show a flat pattern of interaction with other MTs at association distances of 25 and 35 nm.
source: In contrast, non-KMTs show a flat pattern of interaction with other MTs at association distances of 25 and 35 nm.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by data on non-KMT association patterns (Figure 9C).

claim: An increase in the association distance from 35 nm to 50 nm shows a higher tendency of non-KMTs to associate with MTs in the center of the spindle.
source: Moreover, an increase in the association distance from 35 nm to 50 nm, shows a higher tendency of non-KMTs to associate with MTs in the center of the spindle, very likely related to the organization of interpolar MTs in the center of the spindle (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F; Kajtez et al., 2016; Mastronarde et al., 1993; Vukušić et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by data and citations to previous work on interpolar MTs.

claim: KMTs predominantly nucleate de novo at kinetochores, with KMTs growing towards the spindle poles.
source: Combining data on the length and the position of KMT minus ends in spindles (as obtained here by electron microscopy), and the turnover and movement of tubulin in KMTs as generated by light microscopy, a model was proposed in which KMTs predominantly nucleate de novo at kinetochores, with KMTs growing towards the spindle poles.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by reference to a parallel study combining EM and light microscopy data (Conway et al., 2022).

claim: KMTs and non-KMTs are well aligned throughout the spindle.
source: A major outcome of this parallel study is that KMTs in spindles grow along the same trajectories as non-KMTs and that both the KMTs and non-KMTs are well aligned throughout the spindle, leading to the assumption that spindles can be considered as active liquid crystals (Brugués and Needleman, 2014; Oriola et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by reference to a parallel study (Conway et al., 2022) and citations to theoretical work.

claim: Spindles can be considered as active liquid crystals.
source: A major outcome of this parallel study is that KMTs in spindles grow along the same trajectories as non-KMTs and that both the KMTs and non-KMTs are well aligned throughout the spindle, leading to the assumption that spindles can be considered as active liquid crystals (Brugués and Needleman, 2014; Oriola et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion as inference and supported by citations to theoretical work (Brugués and Needleman, 2014; Oriola et al., 2020).

claim: The analyzed spindles show a high nematic order parameter (S = 0.81 ± 0.02) near the chromosomes.
source: Interestingly, the analyzed spindles show a high nematic order parameter (S = 0.81 ± 0.02) near the chromosomes, whereas the nematic order parameter (S = 0.54 ± 0.02) is lower at the spindle poles (Conway et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by reference to measurements from a parallel study (Conway et al., 2022).

claim: The nematic order parameter is lower at the spindle poles (S = 0.54 ± 0.02).
source: Interestingly, the analyzed spindles show a high nematic order parameter (S = 0.81 ± 0.02) near the chromosomes, whereas the nematic order parameter (S = 0.54 ± 0.02) is lower at the spindle poles (Conway et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by reference to measurements from a parallel study (Conway et al., 2022).

claim: KMTs are well aligned in the middle of the spindle, while the order of the KMTs in the k-fibers is progressively lost at positions closer to the spindle poles.
source: Along this line, KMTs in our electron tomography study are well aligned in the middle of the spindle, while the order of the KMTs in the k-fibers is progressively lost at positions closer to the spindle poles.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by the tortuosity and density measurements along k-fibers.

claim: The observed broadening of the k-fibers at the spindle poles might be a direct consequence of a decrease in the internal structural organization of the spindle trajectories.
source: While KMTs are growing out from the kinetochores towards the centrosomes, the observed broadening of the k-fibers at the spindle poles might be a direct consequence of a decrease in the internal structural organization of the spindle trajectories (i.e. of the surrounding non-KMTs).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion as speculation and inferred from the observed correlation between k-fiber broadening and decreased nematic order at poles.

claim: HeLa cells were grown in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS and 100 units/ml of penicillin/streptomycin.
source: HeLa cells (Guizetti et al., 2011) were grown in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle's Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 100 units/ml of penicillin/streptomycin (Pen/Strep).
evidence: This claim is stated in the materials and methods section describing cell culture conditions.

claim: Samples were frozen under high pressure (~2000 bar) with a cooling rate of ~20000°C/s.
source: Samples were frozen under high pressure (~2000 bar) with a cooling rate of ~20000°C/s (Reipert et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is stated in the materials and methods section describing high-pressure freezing and supported by a citation (Reipert et al., 2004).

claim: The border of the MT-centrosome interaction area was defined as 1.7 µm from the mother centriole.
source: To find the edge of this MT-centrosome interaction area, we fit a Gaussian to the distribution peak and defined the cutoff distance for the edge of the MT-centrosome interaction area as twice the half-width, which was 1.7 µm from the mother centriole. (Figure 5B, gray area).
evidence: This claim is stated in the materials and methods section describing the definition of the MT-centrosome interaction area.

claim: MTs with one endpoint found within 100 nm from the border of a reconstructed tomogram were discarded.
source: As also done in our previous study on mitosis in C. elegans (Redemann et al., 2017), we discarded MTs with one endpoint found within 100 nm from the border of a reconstructed tomogram.
evidence: This claim is stated in the materials and methods section describing MT segmentation criteria.

claim: The discarded MTs account for <1% of all traced MTs in all datasets.
source: These discarded MTs account for <1% of all traced MTs in all datasets.
evidence: This claim is stated in the materials and methods section describing the impact of MT exclusion criteria.
